Ransom and redemption language (lytron, apolytrōsis, agorazō) comes from the slave market and from Israel's exodus, when God 'redeemed' his people from Egypt. Early Christians asked a natural question: if a ransom was paid, to whom? Origen answered: to the one who held us captive. Some Fathers rejected any payment to the devil. Gregory of Nazianzus, in his Second Oration on Easter (Oration 45), argued it could be paid neither to the robber nor strictly to the Father, and that the language should not be pressed.

Anselm's Cur Deus Homo (1098) argued that the devil had no rights at all, and the theory declined in academic theology. Yet its narrative of a deceived and defeated enemy survived in liturgy, art and literature, and the modern Christus Victor model reframes it without the devil's 'rights'. C. S. Lewis's The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe (1950), where Aslan dies under the 'Deep Magic' in place of Edmund and rises by a 'deeper magic', is a widely known modern echo. Most patristic writers combined ransom with sacrifice, recapitulation and healing.

Christus Victor ('Christ the Victor') sees the atonement first of all as a divine conflict and triumph. Humanity is held captive by hostile powers: sin, death, the devil, and in some versions the law's curse and the wrath that falls on sin. In Christ, God himself enters the battle; through his life, death and resurrection he defeats these tyrants and liberates the world. The resurrection is not an appendix to the cross but its vindication and the public sign of victory.

Gustaf Aulén named and championed this as the 'classic' view in 1930-31, arguing that it was the dominant view of the Fathers and of Luther, and that it is 'objective' in a different way from Anselm: God is the subject of the whole work from start to finish, not humanity offering satisfaction to God. Modern proponents range from Orthodox and Lutheran theologians to Anabaptists such as J. Denny Weaver, who develop a nonviolent 'narrative Christus Victor', and evangelical Greg Boyd, who sets it within a 'warfare worldview'. Many evangelicals, including N. T. Wright, combine victory with substitution.

Victory imagery runs through the New Testament (the strong man bound, the ruler of this world cast out, the powers disarmed) and through the patristic and liturgical tradition, from Irenaeus to the Orthodox Paschal troparion of Christ trampling down death by death. Aulén argued that Western theology after Anselm replaced this drama with a legal transaction, and that liberal theology reduced it further to moral example.

Critics argued that Aulén oversimplified history, since most Fathers combined several images and Luther strongly affirmed substitution. Still, his book reshaped the discussion. The model was taken up in twentieth-century biblical theology (the 'apocalyptic Paul' of J. Louis Martyn and others), by Pentecostal and Global South Christians attentive to spiritual warfare, and by Anabaptists seeking a nonviolent atonement. Like other models it is commonly held in combination: many argue that substitution is the means and victory the result.

Anselm of Canterbury's satisfaction theory asks why God became human (Cur Deus Homo) and answers by reasoning about sin and justice. Every rational creature owes God the whole obedience of its will; to withhold it is to rob God of the honour due to him, not in the sense of wounding God's ego but of disordering the beauty and justice of creation. Such disorder cannot simply be overlooked. Justice requires either satisfaction (making amends beyond what was taken) or punishment. God, out of mercy, chooses satisfaction rather than the destruction of humanity.

But the debt is infinite and humanity already owes God everything, so no human can pay it, while only a human ought to pay it. Therefore only one who is both God and human can make satisfaction. Christ, being sinless, did not owe death; by freely giving his life he offered a gift of infinite worth that honours God beyond all that sin took away. Such a gift merits a reward, but the Son needs nothing, so the reward is given to those for whom he died, namely forgiveness for all who come to him. Aquinas later refined this into 'superabundant satisfaction' and combined it with merit, sacrifice and redemption, and Catholic teaching continues to use satisfaction language.

7441:
Anselm wrote against two backgrounds. First, he rejected the ransom view's suggestion that the devil had rights over humanity: the devil is a rebel creature and a thief with no just claim. Second, he answered Jewish and Muslim objections that incarnation and crucifixion were unworthy of God, aiming to show 'by necessary reasons' that the God-man was required. Critics since Harnack have read his concept of honour through the lens of feudal society, in which offences against a lord required compensation; defenders argue his 'honour' is the order of justice in creation.

Anselm's argument reshaped Western theology. Aquinas modified it, the Reformers recast it in terms of law and penalty (penal substitution), and Catholic teaching retains it (Trent; Catechism of the Catholic Church 615-616). Anselm explicitly contrasted satisfaction with punishment ('either satisfaction or punishment'), which is a key difference from penal substitution. Like other models it is usually combined with others: Catholic teaching speaks also of sacrifice, redemption, victory and participation.
